blocks.text: Different cutaneous receptors, the receptors of the skin, respond to touch, pressure, heat, cold and pain.

Nociceptors detect pain, defined as a stimulus that causes or is about to cause tissue damage. They are free nerve endings found throughout the body, especially near surfaces; different nociceptors respond to extremes of temperature, very intense pressure or particular chemicals, including some released by injured cells.

blocks.title: Thermoreceptors
blocks.text: Thermoreceptors are naked dendrite endings that detect falls and rises in temperature: cold receptors lie just below the epidermis and warm receptors a little deeper in the dermis. Thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus monitor the temperature of the blood, the body's core temperature.

blocks.alt: A section of skin in three layers, epidermis, dermis and a fat layer, with six numbered receptors: 1 a hair follicle receptor round the root of a hair, 2 free nerve endings reaching into the epidermis, 3 a Merkel cell at the base of the epidermis, 4 a Meissner's corpuscle high in the dermis, 5 a Ruffini ending in the dermis, 6 an onion-like Pacinian corpuscle deep in the fat layer. A key gives what each detects.
blocks.caption: Touch and pain receptors in the skin (original diagram after Figure 15.19).
blocks.long_description: Nociceptors are free nerve endings that detect pain, a stimulus that causes or is about to cause tissue damage; different ones respond to extreme temperature, intense pressure or chemicals released by injured cells. Touch receptors are mechanoreceptors: Meissner's corpuscles (light touch and vibration, in lips, fingertips, palms and soles), hair follicle receptors (hair movement), Merkel cells (light touch, in the deepest epidermis), Pacinian corpuscles (deep pressure and vibration) and Ruffini endings (stretching and sustained pressure).

blocks.text: These receptors send impulses through sensory neurons to the spinal cord and then the brain, where the signals become the sensations of touch.
